entry.title: Nobody Builds a Road to Nowhere
entry.summary: AI data centres use real water, power and land. But infrastructure never grows without limit, and water is about where and when. An optimist's case.
entry.content:
"AI data centers will destroy the planet."

I keep hearing this. And I disagree.

Not because the concerns aren't real. They are. Data centres use water. They use electricity. They take up land. All true, and I'll put numbers on each of them below.

But the doom version of the argument stretches those truths far beyond their proportion. It imagines a straight line going up forever: more chips, more halls, more cooling towers, until the server farm is the planet.

That isn't how infrastructure has ever grown. And it isn't how this will grow either.

First, the honest numbers

I want to start with the facts, because an optimist who skips them isn't an optimist, just someone who hasn't looked.

The International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report estimates that data centres used around 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity. Their consumption has grown about 12% a year since 2017, and the IEA's base case projects it to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030. That last number is a projection, not a measurement, and the IEA's own range for 2035 spans 700 to 1,700 TWh depending on how fast AI is adopted and how quickly efficiency improves. [1]

So yes, it's growing fast. But the same report also says data centres account for around a tenth of global electricity demand growth to 2030, less than industrial motors, air conditioning or electric vehicles. [1]

The bigger story is local. In the United States, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates data centres used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of the country's electricity, and projects 6.7% to 12% by 2028. [2] The IEA notes nearly half of US data centre capacity sits in five regional clusters. [1] A global share of 1.5% can still mean a very large share of one town's grid.

On water, the same LBNL report estimates US data centres directly consumed about 66 billion litres in 2023, mostly for cooling, plus nearly 800 billion litres consumed indirectly through the power stations that generated their electricity. [3]

Those are real numbers. They deserve engineering, not denial. They also don't describe a planet turning into a server farm.

Infrastructure has always had a governor

Look at how the big infrastructure waves actually went.

Electricity arrived and wires went up everywhere. Streets, highways, suburbs, countryside. Roads followed the same story, from the Roman network and the Silk Road to concrete highways. Each wave changed the landscape. Each one cut down trees and altered rivers and habitats. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But farming still happens. Water still flows. People still hike. Planes still take off and land. We didn't fill the earth with power lines or pave the whole planet. We built enough to be useful, and then the building slowed.

Why? Because every one of these things has to be paid for, powered, permitted and placed somewhere. Nobody builds a road to nowhere, because somebody has to pay for it. That constraint is the governor on the engine.

Data centres have this governor built in, and it's already biting. The IEA estimates around 20% of planned data centre projects could be delayed by grid constraints, with new transmission lines taking four to eight years in advanced economies and lead times for transformers and cables doubling in three years. [1] A data centre without a grid connection is an expensive shed.

I want to be precise about what the governor does and doesn't do, though. Economics limits how much gets built. It does not guarantee that what gets built is a good investment. Booms overshoot. Some projects will lose money, and some regions will get more than they needed for a while. The claim I'm making is narrower: physical and financial limits stop the expansion long before "everything". They always have.

"Data centres waste water"

This is the argument I hear most, and I think it's both right and wrong.

Here's what's right about my instinct. The water on this planet isn't going anywhere. It cycles: ocean, atmosphere, rain, ground, river, ocean again. A data centre does not delete water from the Earth.

Here's what that instinct misses. Hydrologists don't measure water use by whether water leaves the planet. The US Geological Survey defines consumptive use as the part of withdrawn water that is "evaporated, transpired, incorporated into products or crops, consumed by humans or livestock, or otherwise removed from the immediate water environment." [4]

That word immediate is the whole point. When a cooling tower evaporates water in a dry basin in summer, that water really does come back as rain. Just not necessarily there, and not necessarily this year. For the farms and homes drawing on the same aquifer, it's gone.

So I'd put my original point more carefully. When people say "wasting water", a lot of what they mean is: water that has moved out of reach, and the energy and infrastructure it would take to bring it back. Water goes to the sea? You can desalinate it. Water goes deep underground? You can pump it. Water is dirty? You can treat it.

Energy is a big part of that cost. It isn't the only part. Desalination leaves brine that has to go somewhere. Pipes, plants and permits take years. Ecosystems depend on rivers actually flowing, not just on the water existing somewhere. Cheap energy makes these problems much easier. It doesn't make them disappear.

The engineering is already moving

The more encouraging part is that the industry is designing its way out of the worst of this, and it's doing so because water scarcity has become a cost, a permitting risk and a reputational risk.

Microsoft says that since August 2024 all its new data centre designs use chip-level, closed-loop liquid cooling that evaporates zero water for cooling. The loop is filled once during construction and recirculated. They estimate it avoids more than 125 million litres a year per data centre, with pilots in Phoenix and Wisconsin from 2026. They're also candid about the trade: replacing evaporation with mechanical cooling means "a nominal increase" in annual energy use. [5]

That trade-off is the honest shape of the whole debate.

Evaporative cooling saves electricity and spends water. Closed loops save water and spend some electricity. Reclaimed water or seawater avoids drinking water but needs treatment, pipes and somewhere for the brine or warm discharge to go. Where you build decides which trade makes sense. In a wet, cool climate on a clean grid, it's an easy call. In a desert on a gas-heavy grid, it's a hard one.

That's not a reason for doom. It's a reason to site and design carefully.

Where AI helps the energy problem

Now the part I'm genuinely optimistic about.

I don't think data centres only consume energy. I think AI can help us produce more of it, run it smarter and waste less of it. The IEA, which is hardly a cheerleader, lays out some of the opportunities: [1]

→ AI-based fault detection that can cut outage durations by 30–50%.

→ Sensors and AI management that could unlock up to 175 GW of extra transmission capacity on existing lines, more than the base-case increase in data centre load to 2030.

→ Existing AI applications in buildings that, if scaled up, could save around 300 TWh of electricity, roughly the annual generation of Australia and New Zealand combined.

→ Faster discovery of materials for solar, batteries and carbon capture, where only a tiny fraction of candidate materials has ever been made and tested.

Those are potentials, not results. The IEA is careful to say so, and I want to be too. Its own estimate is that broad use of existing AI solutions could cut emissions by an amount equivalent to about 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035. That's far larger than data centre emissions, and far smaller than what climate change needs. In the IEA's words, AI "is not a silver bullet and does not remove the need for proactive policy." [1]

This is the loop I'm betting on: compute helps make energy cheaper and cleaner, cheaper energy makes water easier to recycle and move, and that supports more compute. It isn't automatic. Every arrow in it needs someone to build something, approve something or pay for something.

The market is the governor. It needs a second hand on it.

I still believe the core of my argument. Nobody builds a data centre they don't expect to pay for itself. Nobody strings power lines to empty land. Financial constraint has always limited infrastructure, and it will limit this.

But I've changed one thing in how I say it. The market limits how much gets built. It doesn't automatically count everything that building costs.

An operator pays for the land, the chips and the electricity at the meter. They don't automatically pay for a drawn-down aquifer in a drought year, a grid upgrade that other customers end up funding, or the emissions of the power mix. Those costs are real, and they only reach the invoice through water pricing, connection rules, planning conditions and disclosure.

That's not an argument against data centres. It's how every infrastructure wave got civilised: roads got environmental reviews, power stations got emission limits, factories got discharge permits. Good rules didn't stop the build. They made it fit.

Where I land

AI data centres are becoming critical infrastructure, like electricity, roads and running water. Saying "data centres are bad for the environment" is a lot like saying "building roads is bad for the countryside". Technically true. Missing most of the point.

So here's my position, as precisely as I can put it.

Will there be growing pains? Yes.

Will there be real environmental impact during the boom, especially in a few concentrated places? Yes.

Will the entire planet become a server farm? No. Power, water, land, capital and permits make sure of that.

Will AI pay back its footprint by making energy and water systems smarter? It can. Whether it does depends on engineering, siting, incentives and governance, not on optimism alone.

The fear is understandable. The doom is disproportionate. We've been here before with electricity, with roads, with every infrastructure leap. We adapted every time, because people did the work of adapting. We'll adapt again the same way.

Where do you stand on the AI infrastructure debate?

Sources

  1. International Energy Agency, Energy and AI: Executive summary (2025). Figures for 2030 and 2035 are IEA projections and scenario ranges.
  2. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley Lab Report Evaluates Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers (January 2025). 2028 figures are scenario ranges.
  3. Shehabi et al., 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (December 2024), section on water.
  4. U.S. Geological Survey, Water-use glossary: consumptive use, and the USGS water cycle diagrams.
  5. Microsoft, Sustainable by design: Next-generation datacenters consume zero water for cooling (December 2024). Company claims, not independent measurements.

All drawings are conceptual illustrations, not to scale and not data.

entry.title: The Cheapest Line Item
entry.summary: The cost of the model thinking is nothing compared to the cost of a wrong answer. Tokens are cheap. Your time is not. Stop optimising for the cheapest line item.
entry.content:
The cost of the model thinking is nothing compared to the cost of a wrong answer.

Let that sink in for a second, because most of the advice going around right now points the other way.

People are out here choosing faster, cheaper models to save a few cents per query. Turning off extended thinking to shave seconds. Picking the lightweight option because "it's good enough."

Good enough for what?

I've been running AI agents on real production work for six months now. Bugs, incidents, investigations, fixes that go out to real users. And the single biggest lesson I've taken from it is almost boring in how obvious it sounds once you say it out loud: the model's thinking time is the cheapest part of the entire pipeline. Everything else around it, especially the humans, costs far more.

What "saving on thinking" actually costs

Here's the scenario I keep seeing. An agent investigates a production bug. It's running on the fast option, or the thinking budget has been turned down, because the investigation "looked simple". It comes back quickly with a confident root cause. The root cause is wrong.

Nothing about that moment feels expensive. The answer arrived in ten seconds. It read well. It sounded sure of itself. The cost doesn't show up there. It shows up over the next several days, one perfectly reasonable step at a time:

→ A fix that addresses the symptom, not the cause.

→ A deploy that doesn't actually fix anything.

→ The same alert firing again three days later.

→ A second investigation from scratch.

→ A second PR, a second review, a second deploy.

→ And whatever customer impact accumulated in between.

What makes this nasty is that every step after the first one is done properly. The fix is well written. The PR is reviewed. The deploy goes out cleanly. The team is doing good work, on the wrong problem. Nobody is being careless. The mistake was made once, at the very top, and everything downstream faithfully inherits it.

And the second investigation is not cheaper than the first. It's usually more expensive, because now you also have to unpick the first theory, explain why the fix didn't work and convince yourself the new answer isn't another confident guess.

Now put that next to what you saved. The "expensive" model that took 90 seconds to think instead of 10? It would have cost you about $0.30 more.

The wrong answer cost you a week.

Let me put actual numbers on this

These are the rough numbers I work with. They're not precise, and they don't need to be, because the gap is so wide that precision doesn't change the conclusion.

→ A senior developer's time: $80-150/hour.

→ A production rollback: 2-4 hours of team time.

→ A wrong root cause that sends you down the wrong path: half a day, minimum.

→ Extended thinking on the best available model: a few cents. Maybe a dollar for a complex investigation.

Do the simple arithmetic on just one of those lines. Half a day is about four hours. At $80-150 an hour, that's roughly $320-600 of one senior developer's time, and that's the minimum, for one person, before anyone else gets pulled in. A rollback is 2-4 hours of team time, so multiply by however many people are in the room for it.

On the other side of the ledger: a few cents. Maybe a dollar.

Even in the most generous framing for the cheap option, a dollar of thinking against a few hundred dollars of one person's half day is a difference of hundreds of times. Stretch that out to the week the wrong answer actually cost, and it isn't worth doing the division.

The economics aren't even close.

And yet people optimise for the cheapest part.

It's like buying the cheapest tyres for a race car. You saved $200 and lost the race. The tyres were never the expensive bit. They were just the bit with a price tag you could see.

That's the trap, I think. Token costs show up on a dashboard, itemised, per query, with a nice graph. The cost of a wrong answer doesn't show up anywhere. It's spread across calendars, standups, a re-opened ticket, a slightly annoyed customer. So people trim the line item they can see and quietly pay the one they can't.

The question that changed my approach

For a while I picked models the way most people do. Which one is cheapest for this? Which one is fast enough? Can I get away with the small one here?

Then I flipped the question. I stopped asking "which model is cheapest?" and started asking:

"What's the cost if this answer is wrong?"

That one question sorts almost every task I give an agent. Here are three from my real work, and all three get the same treatment.

Investigating a concurrency bug in a connection pool that's causing auth failures. That's a top-tier model with max reasoning. Non-negotiable. Concurrency bugs are exactly where a plausible story is easy to tell and hard to verify. Get it wrong and you ship a fix for a race that isn't the race.

Tracing a content visibility leak across three API layers. Same. Full power. A visibility leak means someone is seeing something they shouldn't, or not seeing something they should. The answer has to be right at every layer, not just the first one the model looks at.

Correlating 30 days of error data to measure whether shipped fixes actually worked. Same. This one is sneaky, because it feels like reporting rather than engineering. But the output decides whether we call a problem solved and move on. A wrong "yes, it worked" is how the same incident comes back next quarter with nobody looking for it.

These are high-stakes questions. A wrong answer doesn't just waste tokens. It wastes human time, the most expensive resource in the pipeline.

It doesn't just think longer. It thinks differently.

This is the counterintuitive part, and it's the bit that actually changed my mind rather than just my spreadsheet.

I used to imagine extended thinking as the same answer with extra steps. Same conclusion, more words getting there, a bit more polish. If that were true, turning it off would be a reasonable saving.

It isn't true. Extended thinking is the model considering possibilities it would have skipped in fast mode. Checking its own reasoning. Going back to a piece of evidence and asking whether it really supports the story. Catching the subtle thing that changes the whole picture.

Here's the example that made it click for me.

I've seen an agent in fast mode look at a set of auth failures and confidently say "root cause: connection pool exhaustion", and move on. It's a perfectly reasonable answer. Auth is failing, connections are involved, pools run out. It's the kind of root cause that sounds right in a standup.

Same agent, same problem, with extended thinking, said something different:

"Wait, the pool metrics are normal. The connection that failed was in a subscribed state. This is a pub/sub cleanup race, not a pool issue."

Same logs. Same code. Completely different conclusion. The second one was right.

Look at what that "wait" is doing. It's the model checking its first theory against evidence it already had. The pool metrics were right there. The fast answer simply never went back to look at them, because it had a story that fit well enough. The thinking answer did go back, found the story didn't fit, and then noticed the detail that actually mattered: the state of the connection that failed.

That extra 60 seconds of thinking saved a week of chasing the wrong theory.

If the fast answer had gone out, the likely path is the loop from earlier. Someone tunes the pool. The deploy goes out. The pool metrics, which were already normal, stay normal. The auth failures come back. And then we start again, now with a fix in production that didn't fix anything and needs explaining.

My rule now

So here's where I've landed, and I don't make exceptions to it any more.

If the answer drives a decision, a deploy, or a customer-facing change, use the strongest model at the highest effort. Always. No exceptions.

That doesn't mean everything needs the biggest model. Save the fast, cheap model for the debrief. For formatting. For the parts where accuracy was already established and you just need a summary. I wrote about that split in more detail in Cut to the Chase: let the strong model do the hard thinking, then hand its notes to a fast one to tell me what it found in a few lines. Speed is genuinely valuable there, because the expensive question has already been answered properly.

But for the work that matters? Let the model think.

The tokens are cheap. Your time is not. The wrong answer is the most expensive thing in your workflow.

Stop optimising for the cheapest line item.

What's the most expensive wrong answer you've seen from a "fast" approach?

entry.title: Cut to the Chase
entry.summary: Let the strongest model think as long as it needs. Then hand the debrief to a fast one. Verbose is good at the wrong time and costly at the right one.
entry.content:
Cut to the chase.

Focus is expensive. I don't have time. You don't have time. Nobody has time. And yet most AI output reads like it's being paid by the word.

"Certainly! Here's a comprehensive overview of the potential considerations you might want to take into account when evaluating the various approaches to..."

Stop. I already know the approaches. I evaluated them yesterday. I just need the answer.

For a long time I treated this as a prompting problem. Add "be concise" to the system prompt, add "no preamble", add "don't repeat the question". It helps a little. Then the next task needs real depth, and the same instruction makes the agent cut corners exactly where I didn't want it to. I'd swing the dial back, and the waffle came back with it.

It took me an embarrassingly long time to see that I was trying to fix two different jobs with one setting.

Two completely different modes of work

When I work with AI agents now, almost everything falls into one of two modes, and they need different things from the model.

Mode 1 is the agent doing the hard work. Investigating a production bug. Reading thirty files. Pulling logs. Cross-referencing data. Building a timeline. Writing the fix. Running the tests. Going back when the tests fail.

This is not the time to cut corners. This is the time for maximum reasoning: the strongest model I have access to, the highest effort level, and as long as it needs to think. Let it write ten pages of analysis nobody will read. That's fine. The fluff isn't fluff here. It's the agent reasoning out loud, working through possibilities, eliminating hypotheses. That verbose internal monologue is how it gets to the right answer.

Mode 2 is me making the judgment call. The investigation is done. The analysis exists. The options are laid out. Now I need to understand, decide and move.

This is a debrief, not a discovery session. I don't need the agent to re-explore the entire solution space. I don't need three paragraphs of context I already have. I don't need "Great question!" before the answer. I need three things: here's what we found, here's what it means, here's what I'd do. Done.

That's where "cut to the chase" comes in.

You don't just change the prompt. You change the model.

This was the part that surprised me.

My first instinct was to keep one model and change the instructions between phases. "Now summarise." It works, sort of. But a model tuned to think hard tends to keep thinking hard when you ask it for a summary. It re-opens questions. It hedges. It reaches for completeness because completeness is what made it good at the first job. You end up with a summary that is itself six paragraphs long and still mentions the three hypotheses it already ruled out.

So I split it.

For deep work, I use the strongest reasoning model available and let it run hot. The cost of thinking is nothing compared to the cost of a wrong answer. A wrong root cause on a production incident costs a second incident, a rollback, a weekend, sometimes a customer. Thinking tokens are cheap by comparison, and they get cheaper every few months.

For the debrief, I switch to a fast, articulate model. One that sounds human. Gets to the point. Doesn't pad. Doesn't hedge. Doesn't repeat my question back to me before answering it.

Think about how a good team already works. You wouldn't send your most thorough, methodical engineer to give a two-minute status update to the CTO. That engineer is exactly the person you want on the investigation. They will check the thing everyone else assumed. But ask them for a status update and you get the full history of every theory, in order, because to them the history is the point.

You'd send the person who can summarise a week of work in three sentences without losing the substance. Not because they're smarter. Because that's a different skill, and the CTO's next twenty minutes depend on it.

Same principle. Different model for a different job.

Why the verbose part is not waste

I want to defend the long, rambling part properly, because "AI is too verbose" has become a lazy complaint and it gets aimed at the wrong place.

When an agent investigates, its written-out reasoning is doing real work. It's the scratchpad. "The error started at 14:02. The deploy finished at 13:58. That's suspicious, but the error rate is flat for four minutes after, so maybe not the deploy. Let me check what else changed at 14:00. There's a cron job..." Every one of those sentences is a step that, if skipped, could send the investigation the wrong way. A good engineer does exactly the same thing in their head or on a notepad. We just never had to read it.

Cut that short and you don't get a faster correct answer. You get a faster guess.

So I don't want the deep-work model to be concise. I want it to be thorough, to write its notes down, and to leave them somewhere I can check if I ever need to. I just don't want to be the one reading them by default.

The fluff problem is a timing problem

Here's the reframe that made all of this click for me.

The fluff problem isn't that AI generates too many words. It's that it generates too many words at the wrong time.

During investigation, verbose is good. That's the agent processing. During the debrief, every unnecessary sentence is a tax on human attention.

And human attention is the most expensive resource in the entire pipeline. More expensive than compute. More expensive than tokens. More expensive than the model itself.

Look at what's actually scarce in a working day. I can buy more compute with a credit card in a minute. I can run the investigation again overnight. I can't buy more of my own focus. I get a few good hours a day where I can make careful decisions, and every one of those hours is shared between code review, incidents, design calls and the people I work with. When a debrief burns ten minutes of that on preamble, that's ten minutes I didn't spend deciding something else well.

That picture is deliberately rough. I'm not claiming numbers. The shape is the point. The machine's cost peaks while it investigates, and that's exactly where I want to spend more, not less. My cost peaks at the moment I read the result. That's the only place where cutting words saves anything that matters.

Paragraph six

One more thing most people haven't realised: this isn't just about saving time. It's about decision quality.

When an agent buries the key finding inside paragraph six of a twelve-paragraph response, you're not just slower. You're more likely to miss it.

Be honest about how you read long AI responses. I know how I do. I read the first paragraph carefully. I skim the second. By the fourth I'm reading the first few words of each line, looking for something that sounds like an answer. When I find something that sounds like one, I stop and move on. I pattern-match on the first plausible conclusion.

If the real finding is in paragraph six, and paragraph two contained a plausible-sounding hypothesis the agent later ruled out, I can walk away with the ruled-out one. Not because the agent was wrong. Because the agent was right in the wrong place.

A concise debrief doesn't just respect your time. It forces the important thing to be the first thing you read. That's not a style preference. That's a design decision for better outcomes.

What this looks like on a real bug

Let me make this concrete with an example. It's illustrative, a composite of the kind of incident I've worked many times, not a transcript.

Checkout requests start failing intermittently on a Tuesday afternoon. Around one in fifty orders gets a 502. I hand it to the deep-work agent with the logs, the deploy history, the service map and the repo. Then I go and do something else.

It spends a long time. It reads the load balancer logs and finds the 502s cluster on one upstream. It checks the deploy history: a payment client library was bumped that morning. It reads the library's changelog and finds a default connection pool size went down. It cross-references traffic: the failures line up with the afternoon peak, not with the deploy time. It reads the client code and finds we never set the pool size explicitly. It considers and rules out a DNS change, a certificate rotation and a database lock it found in the logs. It writes a fix that sets the pool size, writes a test, runs the suite. Its notes run to many pages.

Now here are two ways that work can come back to me.

The first is what I used to get by default:

Certainly! I've completed a thorough investigation into the intermittent 502 errors affecting the checkout service. This was a complex issue with several potential contributing factors, so let me walk you through my analysis step by step.

First, I examined the overall error landscape. Errors began on Tuesday afternoon and affected roughly 2% of checkout requests. Initially, I considered whether a recent DNS change could be responsible, since DNS issues often manifest as intermittent upstream failures...

Next, I looked at the database. I noticed some lock waits around the same period, which could plausibly cause timeouts...

(three more paragraphs of eliminated hypotheses)

Interestingly, I found that the payment client library was updated this morning, and the new version reduces the default connection pool size. Since our code doesn't set this explicitly, under peak load...

(two paragraphs of fix details, then "I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions.")

Everything in it is true. The finding is in there. It's just in paragraph six, behind a DNS theory and a database theory, both of which I could easily walk away believing if I'm reading it between two meetings.

The second is the debrief I want:

Finding: The 502s come from the payment client running out of connections at peak. This morning's library upgrade lowered the default pool size, and we never set it ourselves.

What it means: It's not data loss. Failed checkouts weren't charged. It will get worse at the evening peak.

What I'd do: Ship the one-line fix in the PR I opened, which pins the pool size to the old default. It has a test. Then add the pool size to our config so library defaults can't move it again.

Confidence: High. Failures line up with pool exhaustion warnings to the second. Evidence: notes/checkout-502.md, sections 3 and 4.

Not checked: Whether the other two services on the same library are affected. Same risk, lower traffic.

Same investigation. Same facts. One of them I can act on in a minute, standing up. The other I have to read twice and hope I read the right part.

The handoff: notes in a file, debrief in a fixed shape

Here's how I actually wire it, because "use two models" is easy to say and easy to get wrong.

The deep-work agent's last job is to write its notes to a file. Not a summary, the notes: the timeline, the evidence with links to the log lines and commits, every hypothesis and why it was kept or ruled out, the fix, the test results. Markdown is fine. It's for the record, and for the second model.

Then a second, fast model reads that file and produces the debrief. Its instructions are short and strict. Answer in this shape and nothing else: the finding, what it means, what I'd do, how confident you are and why, and what was not checked. First line is the finding. No preamble, no sign-off. Every claim points back at a section of the notes.

There are a few reasons this works better than asking one model to do both.

The file is a clean boundary. The fast model doesn't inherit the deep model's habits, its half-explored branches, or its urge to show its work. It gets a finished body of evidence and one job.

The file outlives the conversation. If I want to check the reasoning, it's there. If I hand the incident to a colleague, I hand them the debrief and the file. The debrief is the front page; the notes are the appendix. That's how good incident reports have always worked. We just used to write both by hand.

And the shape is fixed, so I learn where to look. After a week of debriefs in the same shape, my eyes go straight to "Finding" and "Not checked". That's a small thing that makes a big difference when you read a lot of them.

Cut to the chase is not permission to be wrong

This is the counterintuitive part, and it's the part I care about most.

"Cut to the chase" is not "skip the hard work". It's not "give me the first thing that sounds good". It's the opposite. The agent already did the hard work. It already went through the whole universe of information: the markdown files, the proof, the citations, the progress logs, the test results, the PR descriptions. Cut to the chase means you've done the thinking, now give me the conclusion. Tight. Clean. No ceremony.

But short text has its own failure mode. A confident three-line answer reads as more certain than it is. Padding at least has the side effect of exposing doubt; a tight debrief can hide it. So the guardrails go into the shape itself.

The debrief has to cite where the evidence is. Not "I checked the logs", but which section of the notes, which log query, which commit. If it can't point at evidence, it doesn't get to say it.

It has to state its confidence and the reason for it in a sentence. "High, because the timing matches to the second" is useful. "High" on its own is decoration.

It has to list what was not checked. This is the line I read most carefully. Every investigation has edges, and the most dangerous ones are the ones nobody mentions. A verbose response often hides its gaps in paragraph nine. A good debrief puts them on the page in their own row, where I can't miss them.

And it doesn't get to add anything that isn't in the notes. The fast model is a writer, not a second investigator. If it thinks something's missing, the right move is to say so under "not checked", not to quietly fill the gap with something that sounds right.

With those four rules, short stops meaning shallow. It means compressed, with the compression made visible.

My setup, today

So here's where I've landed.

Deep work goes to the strongest model with maximum effort and as much thinking time as it wants. It writes everything down. I don't read it unless I need to.

The debrief goes to a fast model with a direct tone and zero padding, in the same five-part shape every time, citing the notes.

Two modes. Two models. One workflow. The agent does the hard thinking. I do the hard deciding. Nobody wastes time on ceremony.

I expect the details to change. Models get faster, and the strong ones get better at switching register on their own. Maybe one day a single model will do both jobs well. The principle won't change, though. Thinking should be as long as the problem needs, and the answer should be as short as the reader can afford. Those are two different budgets, and the second one is mine.

Cut to the chase isn't lazy. It's what happens when you respect both the work and the human reading it.

What's your setup? One model for everything, or have you started splitting the modes?

entry.title: The Ticket Title Is Not the Bug
entry.summary: In 1973 Rosenhan showed how a label rewrites every observation after it. Engineers do the same with ticket titles, and AI agents can help us stop.
entry.content:
The ticket said "database issue".

It was assigned to me with a high priority flag, a screenshot of a timeout and a one-line description from someone who had clearly had a bad morning. So I did what I'd been trained to do by years of first-line triage. I opened the database dashboards. I looked at slow query logs. I checked connection pool usage, lock waits and replication lag. Every graph I opened, I read through the lens of that title. A small spike in connections? Suspicious. A query that took longer than usual? Probably related.

It wasn't the database. It was a network timeout between two services, set far too low after a config change, and the database was just the place where the waiting showed up. I'd spent a good chunk of the day collecting evidence for a story somebody else had written in five words.

I've told versions of that story for years as a funny debugging anecdote. Recently I found out a psychologist ran the same experiment on hospitals, fifty years ago, and it isn't funny at all.

Eight people who said one strange thing

In 1973, the Stanford psychologist David Rosenhan published a paper in Science called "On Being Sane in Insane Places". The setup, as he reported it, was simple. Eight people with no history of mental illness, Rosenhan included, phoned psychiatric hospitals and asked for an appointment. At the interview, each said they had been hearing a voice. It was unclear, but it seemed to say "empty", "hollow" and "thud". Apart from a false name and, for the professionals among them, a false job, everything else they said about their lives was true.

All of them were admitted, across twelve hospitals in five states. Seven were diagnosed with schizophrenia and one with manic-depressive psychosis. The moment they were on the ward, they stopped mentioning the voices and behaved normally. They said they felt fine. They were friendly and cooperative.

Nobody on staff spotted them. They stayed between 7 and 52 days, 19 on average, and when they were released it was not as healthy people who had been misjudged. They were discharged with schizophrenia "in remission". The label didn't get removed. It got a status update.

The detail that stuck with me most is small. The pseudo-patients took notes, openly, all day. In one set of records a nurse wrote it down as "patient engages in writing behavior". Ordinary note-taking, observed by a professional, was recorded as a symptom, because the person doing it already had a diagnosis. Meanwhile, in the first three hospitalisations where counts were kept, 35 of the 118 patients on the admissions ward voiced suspicion that the newcomers were sane. "You're not crazy. You're a journalist, or a professor." The people with no authority and no label to protect read the evidence better than the people whose job it was.

The ticket title is a diagnosis

If you've worked in software for any length of time, you have seen "writing behaviour" in a Jira comment.

A ticket comes in labelled "database issue", "frontend bug" or "customer error". From that point on, every log line gets read in the light of that label. Evidence that fits is noted. Evidence that doesn't fit is noise, or a separate issue, or "probably unrelated". The title is written once, often by the person with the least information, at the moment of maximum panic, and then it quietly becomes the frame for everyone downstream.

We have a whole vocabulary of labels that work like this. A test marked "flaky" stops being investigated. When it fails, people hit retry, and the one time it fails because of a real race condition, nobody looks, because it's the flaky one. A module tagged "legacy" gets blamed for anything odd that happens near it. "Works as intended" closes a conversation that might have been the first report of a real design problem. "Won't fix" turns into a reason to dismiss the next report that looks similar, even when it isn't.

People get labels too. A pull request from a contributor everyone considers senior and careful gets a lighter review. The same change from someone tagged "junior" gets picked apart line by line.

And the reporter's framing sticks harder than anything. "The export is broken" sends you to the export code. "The export is slow since Tuesday" sends you to Tuesday's deploy. Same bug, two different investigations, decided before anyone has looked at a single log line.

Rosenhan's point, at least as he framed it, was that once the label was applied, the behaviour stopped being information. That's the failure mode I care about as an engineer. The first label isn't a problem in itself. We have to call the ticket something. The problem is when the label stops being a hypothesis and starts being the lens.

The hospital that caught impostors who didn't exist

The second part of the paper is the one I find most useful for engineers, and it's also the part that tends to get slightly garbled when the story is retold.

After the first results came out, a research and teaching hospital told Rosenhan that kind of mistake couldn't happen there. So he made them an offer. Over the next three months, he said, one or more pseudo-patients would try to get admitted. Staff should rate every new patient on how likely they were to be an impostor.

Out of 193 patients, 41 were judged with high confidence to be pseudo-patients by at least one staff member. Twenty-three were considered suspect by at least one psychiatrist. Nineteen were suspected by both a psychiatrist and another staff member. Rosenhan had sent nobody. Note that's 41 flagged by someone, not 41 the hospital agreed on, but it's still a lot of alarms about a problem that wasn't there.

Anyone who has tuned monitoring will recognise this immediately. Tell an on-call team "we think someone is attacking the login endpoint this week" and watch the false positives roll in. Every slightly odd IP is suspicious. Every burst of failed logins is the attack. You haven't made them better at detecting attacks. You've changed their threshold. Rosenhan himself framed it in terms of errors: the first study showed the hospitals leaning hard towards calling healthy people sick, and the second showed that if you raise the stakes, you can push staff to lean the other way. Neither shows a well-calibrated detector. Every alert tuned too sensitive, and every label like "it's always the database", moves the threshold the same way. (A small nerd aside: in the paper he calls the false positive a "Type 2" error, which is the opposite of how most statisticians label it today. Even the error labels in the famous paper about labels are swapped.)

What's contested, and why I'm still telling the story

Here's the part the short versions of this story usually leave out, and I think it matters.

The Rosenhan study has come under serious criticism. Critics at the time, most famously the psychiatrist Robert Spitzer, pointed out that if you lie convincingly about a symptom, a doctor treating you for that symptom isn't proof that diagnosis is broken. Seymour Kety put it as: if he drank a quart of blood and showed up vomiting it, nobody would conclude medicine can't diagnose ulcers. That's a fair hit.

Then, in 2019, the journalist Susannah Cahalan published The Great Pretender, after going through Rosenhan's private papers. She found inconsistencies between his records and the published paper, and she could only identify two of the eight pseudo-patients for certain. One of them, a graduate student, described his experience differently from how it appeared in the study, and his data seems to have been left out. Records she found suggest that at least one pseudo-patient, by her account Rosenhan himself, told the admitting doctor more than just "thud". Nature's review of the book summarises the trail, and in 2023 the historian Andrew Scull went further and called the study a "successful scientific fraud" in the journal History of Psychiatry. Those claims are disputed and can't be fully settled now that Rosenhan is gone, but the honest summary is that the study's details aren't trustworthy enough to carry the weight it has been given.

The second experiment has its own catch. Since no fake patients were sent, it can't tell you anything about whether staff could detect real impostors. What it shows is how expectations and incentives change what people flag, which is useful, but it's a different and smaller claim than "psychiatrists can't tell the sane from the insane".

And yet the paper landed at a moment when American psychiatry already knew its diagnoses were unreliable, and it added a lot of pressure. Spitzer, one of its sharpest critics, went on to lead the work on DSM-III in 1980, which moved psychiatric diagnosis towards explicit, checkable criteria. The Wikipedia article on the experiment covers both the influence and the criticism well.

I find that whole arc strangely fitting. A famous study about how labels distort evidence was itself carried for decades by its label: "landmark experiment", "Stanford", "Science". Plenty of people, me included, repeated it without checking the records. The fix was the same as for any bad ticket: someone went back and read the primary evidence instead of the summary.

Where AI agents come in

I use AI coding agents every day, and I'm strongly in favour of them. So I want to be precise about where they fit here, because "AI hallucinates, AI is biased" is the lazy take.

An agent given a wrong label behaves a lot like a tired engineer given a wrong label. Hand it a ticket titled "database issue" and a plan that starts with "check the slow queries", and it will check the slow queries. If it finds something slightly odd, it will often build an explanation around it. If it hits evidence that doesn't fit, it can explain that away too, with complete confidence and very good grammar. It didn't invent that frame. It inherited it from the ticket, from the docs, from our runbooks and from the label we wrote at the worst possible moment.

But there are two important differences, and both are good news.

First, an agent has no ego in the outcome. It didn't write the ticket. It doesn't have a reputation as "the database person" to defend, and it won't be embarrassed to say the senior engineer's diagnosis was wrong. I've written before about ego running production. Agents don't fix that problem in us, but they don't add to it either.

Second, an agent will happily start again from scratch, as many times as you ask, which is the thing humans are worst at. Once I've spent three hours on the database theory, I'm invested. Ask an agent to drop everything and re-read the evidence, and it just does it.

So I've changed how I hand over investigations. Instead of passing the ticket title through as the goal, I'll often say: ignore the title and the reporter's guess. Here are the logs, the deploy history and the error timeline. Tell me what you think is happening, and what evidence would prove you wrong. Then, separately, I'll ask it to evaluate the original label against what it found. Two passes, one with the label and one without, and I compare.

This is the same lesson I keep relearning: the quality of the ask decides the quality of the answer. A vague or loaded ask gets a loaded answer. It's also why I like giving agents the boring parts of the job, like pulling thirty days of logs and lining up the timeline. That's exactly the work that a rushed human skips, and skipping it is how a label survives unchallenged.

And I review the evidence, not just the conclusion. An agent's summary that says "root cause: connection pool exhaustion" is a label too. What I want to see underneath is the log lines, the timestamps and the graph that shows it. If the evidence doesn't support the conclusion, the conclusion goes, no matter how confidently it's written.

Re-reading from scratch

Rosenhan's wards, real or exaggerated, had no cheap way to re-read a patient from zero. Every observation went into a chart that already had a diagnosis at the top. Our systems are the same if we let them be: the ticket title sits at the top, every comment below is written in its shadow, and the post-mortem often ends up confirming the first guess because that's the story everyone already told.

We can design against it. Treat the first label as a hypothesis with an owner and a timestamp, not a fact. Let the post-mortem say "the initial triage label was wrong, and here's how that slowed us down" without blaming anyone. Retire "flaky" as a permanent tag and make it expire. Review the trusted contributor's diff with the same care as the new person's. And use agents for what they're unusually good at: looking at the same evidence again, with no memory of the story we've been telling ourselves.

The patients on those wards saw through the label because they weren't invested in it. A good agent, given clean context, can be that outside voice for us. It still needs a human to decide what matters. But it can read "writing behaviour" and say what nobody on the ward would: that's just someone taking notes.

What sent me down this rabbit hole was a short video by Reni B-Alfred about the experiment. It's worth four minutes. The facts above come from the paper and the sources linked, and the criticism is worth reading as closely as the story.

entry.title: Give the Boring Parts of Software Engineering to AI
entry.summary: The boring parts of engineering get rushed: logs, legacy code, PR descriptions, week-after checks. I hand them to an agent and keep the decisions.
entry.content:
Nobody talks about the boring parts of software engineering.

They don't make it into tech talks or blog posts. Nobody gives a conference keynote on how they pulled thirty days of logs to find when an error started, or how they read four hundred lines of legacy code to work out why one flag exists. And yet, by my estimate, this stuff is about 70% of the job.

It's also the part most engineers rush through. I know because I did it for years.

This post is about what changed when I stopped doing the boring parts myself and handed them to my agentic workflow. All of them. Not because I want to do less work, but because the boring work finally gets done properly, and I get to spend my own attention on the bit that actually needs a human.

What the boring parts actually look like

When people imagine software engineering, they picture the interesting part: designing a system, writing a clever fix, arguing about architecture on a whiteboard. That part is real, but it's the thin end of the week. Here's the rest, in generic terms.

Pulling 30 days of logs to find when an error started. A customer reports something broken. The error rate graph looks a bit higher than usual, but it's noisy. Did this start with last Tuesday's deploy? With a config change? With a third-party API that quietly changed its response format? The answer is in the logs, spread across a month and a few services, and finding the first occurrence means filtering, grouping, exporting, and squinting at timestamps in two different timezones.

Cross-referencing three databases to trace one customer's broken state. The orders table says the payment went through. The billing service says it didn't. The analytics warehouse has a third opinion. Somewhere between them is the moment this customer's account went wrong, and the only way to find it is to pull the same customer's rows from each system, line them up by time and spot where the story stops making sense.

Reading 400 lines of legacy code to understand why a flag exists. There's a boolean called something like skip_legacy_sync that's checked in a dozen places. Nobody on the team remembers who added it. The person who did left years ago. Before you can safely remove it, or even safely change the code around it, you have to read everything that touches it and reconstruct the reason from the code itself, the commit history and whatever tickets still exist.

Writing the PR description that nobody will read but everyone will need later. The fix is done. The tests pass. Now you have to write down what changed, why, what you considered and rejected, how you verified it and what to watch afterwards. Today, the reviewer will skim it. A year or two from now, someone running git blame at midnight during an incident will need every word of it.

Checking if the fix actually reduced errors a week after shipping. This is the one that almost never happens. You shipped the fix, closed the ticket and moved on. Did the errors actually go down? Or did they drop for a day and creep back, because the real cause was something else? Finding out means going back to the dashboards a week later, comparing before and after, and writing it up. By then you're three tickets deep into something else.

None of this is glamorous. All of it matters.

Why the boring work gets rushed

It's not because engineers are lazy. I've worked with plenty of engineers and very few of them were lazy. The boring work gets rushed because engineers are human.

We get tired. Correlating log lines at four in the afternoon is not the same as doing it at nine in the morning. By the third hour, you start skimming. You see a pattern that fits your theory and you stop looking for the one that doesn't.

We context switch. There are always three other tickets open, a review waiting, a Slack thread asking for an update. Every interruption resets the careful mental model you were building of that legacy module, and rebuilding it costs more each time.

We're under ticket pressure. The visible output of the job is the fix. The investigation behind it, the description around it and the follow-up after it don't show up on a board. So when time is short, those are the first things to get trimmed.

And honestly, we want to get to the interesting part, so we pay the price of admission as quickly as we can. That's when shortcuts creep in: the timeline that's "probably" right, the legacy code we read half of, the PR description that just says "fixes the export bug", the week-after check that never happens.

Why it matters more than it looks

The cost of rushing the boring work doesn't show up straight away. It shows up later, and usually on someone else's afternoon.

A rushed investigation means a fix for the wrong cause. The symptom goes away for a while, the ticket closes, and the real problem comes back next month with a new ticket number. A half-read legacy module means the flag you removed was load-bearing for some edge case nobody remembered, and now that edge case is an incident.

A thin PR description is a debt the whole team pays. Code tells you what it does. Only the description, written at the time, tells you why it was done that way and what else was tried. When that's missing, the next engineer has to redo the investigation from scratch, or worse, guesses.

And skipping the week-after check means you never actually know whether your work helped. You think it did. You moved on believing it did. That's a quiet kind of overconfidence, and it's the same trap I wrote about in ego in production: certainty that nobody ever asked you to prove.

The boring parts are where the evidence lives. Skip them and you're doing engineering by vibes.

What I hand to the agent

AI doesn't get tired. It doesn't rush because it has three other tickets open. It doesn't skip the last week of logs because it's nearly home time. It's not perfect, and I'll come back to that, but it is relentlessly thorough in exactly the places where I used to cut corners.

So I gave my agentic workflow the boring work. In practice the instructions are short and blunt, because I've learnt that clear asks get clear results.

For the logs, it's roughly: pull the logs, correlate them, show me the timeline. The agent queries the last thirty days across the services involved, finds the first occurrence of the error, lines it up against deploys and config changes, and hands me a timeline with the actual log lines and queries attached. Not a summary I have to trust, but the raw evidence behind each step.

For the broken customer, it's the same shape: pull the records from each system, line them up by time, show me where they disagree. An afternoon of copy-pasting between query windows becomes one table.

For legacy code: read it, explain what it does, tell me what breaks if I change it. The agent reads every call site of that flag, the commits that touched it and any linked tickets it can find, then writes a plain-language explanation and a list of the paths that would behave differently if the flag went away. It reads all four hundred lines. Every time. I used to read the first hundred carefully and the rest hopefully.

For the PR: write the description, include the evidence, link the dashboards. By the time the fix is ready, the agent has already been part of the investigation, so it knows what we found, what we ruled out and why. The description it drafts has the timeline, the root cause, the alternatives we rejected, how we tested it and the links to the graphs that prove it. I edit it, but I'm editing a complete draft, not staring at an empty text box at the end of a long day.

And for the follow-up: check the error rates next week, compare before and after, write the report. This is the one I'm happiest about, because it's the one I used to skip entirely. A week after the fix ships, the agent pulls the same metrics for the same window before and after, compares them and writes a short report. Sometimes the report says the fix worked. Sometimes it says the errors dropped but a related one went up. Either way, I find out, instead of assuming.

The guardrails

I'm very pro-AI, but I'm not naive about it. Agents make mistakes. They misread a timestamp, pick the wrong join key, or confidently explain code that does something slightly different from what they said. So the way I work has a few rules that never bend.

The agent gets read-only access for this kind of work. It can query logs, read databases through read-only credentials and browse the code and dashboards. It doesn't change production data, deploy anything or close tickets on its own. Investigation is reading, so the access is reading.

I verify the evidence, not just the conclusion. That's why I ask for the raw log lines and the queries, not just the timeline. If the agent says the errors started at a particular deploy, I open that deploy and the first few log lines myself. It takes minutes, because the agent has already done the hours of searching.

I spot-check the correlation. Things happening at the same time aren't always cause and effect. When the agent lines up an error spike with a deploy, I ask what else changed in that window, and I sometimes ask it to argue the opposite case. A good timeline survives that.

And the agent proposes, the human decides. It can tell me what the flag does and what breaks if I remove it. It doesn't decide whether to remove it. It can draft the PR description. I decide whether it's true before it goes out under my name.

Checking evidence is much faster than gathering it, and that's the whole trick.

The part that actually needs a human

So what do I do with the time I get back?

The part that was always the actual job: deciding what to fix, how to fix it and whether the trade-offs are worth it.

Deciding what to fix means looking at the timeline and the customer impact and choosing. Is this worth fixing properly now, or patching and scheduling? Is it even the most important problem this week? An agent can lay out the evidence, but it doesn't know that the finance team is mid-audit, or that this customer is about to renew, or that the team is stretched thin this sprint.

Deciding how to fix it means weighing options with judgement and context. A quick guard clause, or the refactor the module has needed for years? A data migration now, or a backfill later? These calls depend on people, timing and risk appetite as much as on code.

And deciding whether the trade-offs are worth it is the most human part of all. Every fix costs something: review time, deploy risk, a bit more complexity, a behaviour change someone depends on. Saying "yes, this is worth it" or "no, leave it alone" is a judgement call, and I'd rather make it with a clear head and complete evidence than after three hours of squinting at logs.

There's a broader point here too. In the middleman post I argued that the gap between a powerful tool and the people who need it doesn't close by itself. The same is true inside an engineering team. Agents produce the evidence. Someone still has to turn that evidence into the right decision for this team, this product and this week.

The result

The boring work actually gets done now. Properly. Every time.

The timelines are complete instead of probably right. The legacy code gets read end to end. The PR descriptions are good enough that future me will be grateful. And the week-after check happens, which means I actually know whether my fixes worked, rather than hoping they did.

Automate the boring parts

There's a lot of excitement about AI doing the fun parts of engineering: generating whole features, designing systems, writing the clever bit. But I think the engineers who'll really win with AI aren't the ones who automate the fun parts.

They're the ones who automate the boring parts and do the fun parts better.

Hand the agent the logs, the cross-checks, the legacy code, the PR description and the follow-up. Give it read-only access, check its evidence and keep the decisions for yourself. Then spend your own energy on the part that actually needs a human.

What's the most tedious part of your workflow that you'd hand to an AI today?

entry.title: Why You Rarely Hear Live Singing in Small Indian Venues
entry.summary: Why small Indian cafes rarely have live singers: an average Tamil film song needs two vocalists and a ten-piece band, while a pop song needs a guitar.
entry.content:
This one is off topic. No Django, no Kubernetes, no AI agents. Just something that has been bugging me for years, every time I walk into a small bar or cafe overseas and there's a guy in the corner with a guitar, singing his heart out to forty people and a coffee machine.

Why don't we have that in India?

I don't mean concerts. India has huge concerts, film music nights, temple festivals and wedding bands. I mean the small, everyday version: a Friday night in a neighbourhood cafe, two or three musicians, a mic stand and a tip jar. Travel a bit and you'll see it everywhere. In Chennai or Bangalore it exists, but it's much rarer, and when it does happen it's usually not Tamil film songs.

My theory: it's not about talent or taste. It's about arithmetic. Faithfully reproducing even an average Tamil film song takes a big band, and a big band costs money that a small venue doesn't have.

Indian film songs are complex at the foundation

Let me say the part that surprises a lot of Western friends. On a foundation level, Indian film songs are very complex.

Don't get me wrong. Complex Western songs exist. Queen exists. Prog rock exists. Jazz will happily melt your brain. But the default Western pop or rock song is built to be carried by a few people. The default Tamil film song is built in a studio, by a composer with an orchestra at his disposal, for a scene in a movie, and nobody involved was thinking about whether three people in a cafe could play it later.

Take an ordinary example. Not a Rahman masterpiece, not an Ilaiyaraaja symphony. Just a regular, well-loved album: Yuvan Shankar Raja's soundtrack for Yaaradi Nee Mohini (2008), the Dhanush and Nayanthara film. Put on "Oru Naalaikkul" and actually listen to everything happening underneath the vocals. Then imagine reproducing it faithfully, live, in a room the size of a living room.

My first instinct is to say you'd need a 200-member band. Okay, 200 is a stretch. But you will not get anywhere near the record with two people. Let's count properly.

You need two singers before you play a single note

Most Indian film songs are duets. Whether you agree with that or not, it's the reality of the catalogue. There's a male portion, there's a female portion, and they trade lines, verses and sometimes whole stanzas. "Oru Naalaikkul" is Karthik and Rita. "Nenjai Kasakki" on the same album is Udit Narayan and Suchitra.

And here's the funny part: you can't just have one singer cover both. A man can't really sing the female portion, and the other way round sounds odd too. The keys sit in different ranges, and because most of these duets are romantic, it gets awkward fast when one person is singing both sides of a love conversation. It's like a one-man play of a wedding proposal.

Long story short: one male vocalist, one female vocalist. Period. That's two people on the payroll and we haven't touched an instrument.

Then the instruments

Here's the smallest band I can imagine that would get through a typical Tamil film song without the audience wincing:

  • Flute. So much of the melodic colour lives in the flute lines between verses. Without it the interludes are empty.
  • Tabla. The rhythmic feel of a lot of songs comes from tabla or a similar hand percussion, not a drum kit.
  • Keyboard or piano. The workhorse. A good keyboardist covers strings, pads, bells and half the orchestra with patches.
  • Guitar. Rhythm parts, and often a lead line or solo.
  • Drum pads. Most bands don't bring a full acoustic kit anymore, and that's fine. Electronic pads are highly versatile and can trigger almost any sound.

That's seven people including the two singers. Now the "you really should have" list:

  • Congas or triple drums, because so many songs have a percussion section that tabla and pads don't quite nail.
  • Bass guitar, because the low end matters more than people think.
  • A dedicated lead guitar, separate from rhythm.
  • Violin, for the string lines a keyboard patch only imitates.

And the "nice to have, but forget about it" list: nadaswaram for the songs that need it, and veena if you're feeling ambitious. You don't need them for every song, but when a song does, nothing else sounds the same.

Some people try to play tabla on the pads too. You can, and good players get close, but it isn't real tabla. The bols, the bends from the left-hand drum, the way the sound breathes: a sample doesn't do all of that.

Add it up and you land somewhere around ten people for a respectable version. Some parts can be folded into the keyboard, and that's fine, but I genuinely can't picture a Tamil live band that does justice to film songs with fewer than about ten members. For the full experience, think closer to twenty.

Two separate lanes: singers and players

Meanwhile, in plenty of places I've travelled, I've seen two-piece and three-piece acts holding a room. And very often the person singing is also the person playing guitar.

That's something you rarely see with Indian musicians, and I think there's a real reason for it. Indian vocals, Tamil film vocals included, are demanding. A huge number of our singers trained classically for years and dedicated their whole lives to the voice alone. Think about how many top Indian playback singers you've seen holding a guitar on stage. Not many. Playing an instrument at a high level is its own lifelong discipline, and singing at that level is another one. So it becomes two separate lanes.

In the West, the singer-songwriter with a guitar is practically an archetype. Ed Sheeran builds entire stadium sets out of one voice, a guitar and a loop pedal. Bruno Mars sings while playing. In a lot of Western bands the guitarist sings, the keyboard player sings, and sometimes even the drummer sings. One person covering two jobs halves the headcount, and that changes the economics of a small gig completely.

To be fair, it's not because Western singing is easy. A great pop vocal is hard. It's that the songs are usually designed so the voice and a couple of instruments can carry them.

Biryani versus a sandwich

The more you listen, the more you realise an Indian film song is like a biryani. There are layers and layers. Rice, masala, meat, fried onions, saffron, mint, a dozen spices doing their own thing, and somehow it all has to come together at once.

A typical English pop song is more like a sandwich. Toast two slices of bread, put something good inside, done. And I say that with love. A great sandwich is a great meal, and nobody complains that a sandwich isn't a biryani.

There's a running meme online where someone proudly shows a "perfect meal" and an Indian person replies, roughly, "Perfect meal? That's just the prep work. Where does the cooking start?" That's exactly the gap I'm talking about, applied to music.

Where the richness actually comes from

Now let me correct my own brainstorm, because my first take was unfair.

It's tempting to say Western music is "flat" and "just twelve semitones". That's not quite right. Indian music uses the same twelve-note octave as its working frame; the harmonium and keyboard that half our film industry runs on are tuned to it. The richness isn't in having more notes. It's in what you do between and around them:

  • Raga grammar. A raga isn't just a scale. It has rules for how you approach and leave notes, which phrases belong to it and which notes to emphasise.
  • Gamakas. The ornaments, slides and oscillations that make a note move. A note in Carnatic music is often more of a gesture than a fixed point.
  • Shrutis. The finer pitch shades that theory recognises within the octave, which singers use for intonation and expression.
  • Tala. Rhythmic cycles that percussionists play with, around and against.
  • Layered orchestration. Film composers stack all of the above with strings, synths, folk percussion and choir.

Western music has its own depth, especially in harmony. Chord progressions, voice leading and counterpoint are where a lot of its richness sits. Popular Western songs just tend to be lighter on layers by design, and that is precisely why they travel so well into small rooms. A strummed chord progression can carry a song. A raga-based melody with orchestral interludes can't be carried by strumming alone.

Different recipes, not better and worse cooks.

So it comes down to money

Here's where it lands. If a cafe wants a two-piece, that's two people to pay, two people to feed and a corner of the room. If it wants a Tamil film band that won't get booed, it needs:

  • A bigger group, so a much bigger total fee.
  • A bigger space, with room for ten musicians, their gear and a proper sound system.
  • A bigger crowd, to justify all of that on a Friday night.

And the audience is unforgiving. Everyone in the room knows the original recording note for note. Try a thin cover of a beloved song with one guitar and the missing flute line and percussion break are obvious. It sounds flat, and you'll be booed off stage. So the small venues mostly don't bother. They play recorded music or hire a DJ, and live film music moves to bigger venues, weddings, college culturals and ticketed shows, where the budget exists.

The honest counterpoints

I don't want to overstate this, because small live music in India does exist.

  • Unplugged and acoustic covers of Tamil and Hindi songs are popular, especially online and in some cafes.
  • Ghazal nights have always been intimate: a singer, a harmonium, a tabla, often in small rooms.
  • Carnatic concerts in Chennai's sabhas, especially during the December music season, are often small ensembles: a vocalist with violin and mridangam.
  • Indie bands in Bangalore, Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and the Northeast play small venues all the time, usually their own songs, often in English.
  • Karaoke and backing-track nights are a whole culture of their own.
  • Folk traditions across India have performed with small groups for centuries.

And simplicity isn't inferior. Some of my favourite live moments anywhere have been one person and one instrument.

There are also ways a small act can make Tamil film songs work:

  • Reduced arrangements that keep the hook and drop the orchestra.
  • Acoustic reinterpretations, where the point is a new take, not a copy.
  • Backing tracks for the parts you can't staff, with live vocals and one or two live instruments on top.
  • Loop pedals, the Ed Sheeran trick, to layer parts live.
  • A really strong keyboardist, who is honestly worth three people.

The catch is that each of these changes the promise. You're no longer selling "the song you love, played live". You're selling "a new version of the song you love". Some audiences love that. Many still want the biryani.

My take

Small venues in India rarely have live singers because our songs are built for a full kitchen, our singers and instrumentalists usually work in separate lanes, and a ten-piece band is expensive. That's not a weakness. It's the price of a musical tradition that layers everything.

I'd still love to see more small acts try the reinterpretation route, with a keyboardist, a tabla player and two good singers. A smaller biryani, not a sandwich.

If you've been to a small venue in India that pulls this off, tell me where. And if you're a musician who has tried, how small did you manage to make the band?

entry.title: AI Made Me a Better Engineer by Exposing How Vague I Was
entry.summary: Agents read tickets literally, so vague asks get vague code. The ticket, acceptance-criteria, assumption and edge-case habits that made me a better engineer.
entry.content:
Unpopular opinion: AI made me a better engineer.

Not because it writes code for me. It does write a lot of my code, and I'm glad it does. The bigger change happened before any code got written. Working with AI agents every day forced me to get clear about what I actually want, and that turned out to be a skill I'd been quietly faking for years.

I used to get away with vague

For most of my career I could be vague and nobody noticed. I could hold half a plan in my head, start coding and work the rest out as I went. A ticket that said "fix the export" was fine, because I was the one fixing it. The missing detail lived in my head, and nobody could see inside my head to question it.

Teammates covered for it too. A good senior engineer reads a sloppy ticket, fills the gaps from context and gets on with it. A junior messages you three times on Slack. Either way the work gets done eventually, and the cost of the vagueness is spread across other people's afternoons, where nobody counts it.

An agent doesn't absorb that cost. It needs precision, context and a clear definition of done. It reads what you wrote, not what you meant. When I give it vague instructions, I get vague results. Every time.

That isn't a complaint about agents. It's the most honest feedback on my own writing I've ever had.

Vague versus agent-ready

Here's an illustrative ticket, the kind I'd have written a few years ago without a second thought:

Title: Fix order export

The CSV export is broken for big customers. Please fix.

Give that to an agent and you'll get something. Maybe it adds pagination. Maybe it bumps the gunicorn timeout. Maybe it rewrites the export as a background job and invents an email notification nobody asked for. Each one is a reasonable reading of "fix". None of them is guaranteed to be the one I had in my head.

Here's the same ticket, again illustrative, written so an agent or a new teammate can actually finish it:

Title: Order CSV export times out for accounts with 10k+ orders

Context
  /admin/orders/export/ builds the whole CSV inside the request.
  Large accounts hit the 30s load balancer timeout and get a 504.

Goal
  Large exports finish reliably. Small exports stay instant.

Acceptance criteria
  - Under 10k orders: the CSV downloads in the request, as today.
  - 10k or more: the export runs as a Celery task. The user sees
    "We'll email you a link" and gets a download link valid for 24h.
  - Columns, column order and date format are unchanged.
    Finance imports this file.
  - Tests cover both paths and the 10k boundary.

Out of scope
  - New columns or filters. Any other export.

Assumptions (confirm or correct)
  - The existing Celery worker and S3 bucket can be reused.
  - Dates stay in the account's timezone, as they are now.

The second version took about ten minutes. It isn't a spec document. But look at what writing it forced me to decide: where the threshold sits, what the user sees, what must not change, and what I'm not asking for. Someone was always going to make those decisions. The only question was whether I'd make them on purpose or the agent would make them by accident.

Four habits that stuck

Once I started treating agents as literal readers, four habits followed. None of them is new. I just stopped skipping them.

Better ticket descriptions, because the agent reads them literally. Context, goal, scope. When a word could mean two things ("fix", "clean up", "support", "handle"), I replace it with what I actually mean.

Acceptance criteria up front, because the agent checks them. This changed the most. Here's the template I use now:

Done when:
  - [observable behaviour] happens when [condition]
  - [existing behaviour] is unchanged
  - [error case] returns [message or status code], not a 500
  - tests cover [main path], [boundary] and [failure]
Not done if:
  - [something that looks done but isn't]
    e.g. only works with the local seed data

"Not done if" is the underrated part. It catches the agent declaring victory early, and it catches me doing the same.

Documented assumptions, because the agent doesn't guess, it asks. A good agent stops and asks when something is unclear, and every question it asks points at a gap I left. So I write the assumptions down first. An illustrative log from a performance investigation:

Assumptions: slow checkout investigation
  A1  It started with Tuesday's deploy.       CONFIRMED  (APM graph)
  A2  It only affects card payments.          WRONG      (PayPal too)
  A3  The new discount query is the cause.    OPEN       (profiling next)
  A4  No migration went out that day.         CONFIRMED  (deploy log)

Writing A2 down is what made it checkable. In my head it was a fact. On paper it was a guess, and it was wrong. This is the same trap I wrote about in ego in production: certainty that outruns the evidence, because nothing ever asked me to prove it.

Edge cases before code, because the agent will find them anyway. An agent writing tests will happily throw empty lists, odd timezones and Unicode at your code. I'd rather think about them before it does. My pre-flight for most backend changes:

  • Empty, one, many. Zero rows, exactly one, more than a page.
  • Boundaries. The threshold itself, and one either side of it.
  • Time. Timezones, midnight, month end and the DST changeover.
  • Bad input. Missing fields, wrong types, Unicode names, very long strings.
  • Concurrency. Double clicks, retries, two workers picking up the same job.
  • Permissions. The user who shouldn't see this, and the admin who should.
  • Failure. The third-party API is slow, down or returns rubbish.
  • Rollback. What happens to data the new code wrote if we revert.

The spill-over I didn't expect

Six months in, the surprise isn't the agent work. It's everything around it.

My MR descriptions are better. They say what changed, why, and how to check it, because I'm used to writing exactly that for an agent. My investigation reports are more thorough, because the assumptions log is already sitting there when I write them up. My test coverage is tighter, because the edge cases were on paper before the first line of code.

Not because AI does those things for me. Because working with AI made me realise how sloppy I'd been doing them before.

The irony

Here's the uncomfortable bit. The engineers who complain "AI doesn't understand what I want" are often the same engineers who skip writing requirements, leave ticket descriptions blank and expect teammates to just figure it out.
